progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Dm | B♭ C | Dm Dm |
intro: Eighteen verses, the longest of the fifteen Songs of Ascents, and the only one built on two oaths that answer each other. In the first half a man swears he will not sleep until he has found God a place; in the second half God swears back, to David, about a throne. Verses 8 to 10 turn up almost word for word at the close of Solomon's dedication prayer in 2 Chronicles 6, which is the clearest sign of where the psalm belonged. Watch the verb for clothing: it is asked for in verse 9, granted in a changed form in verse 16, and turned against the enemies in verse 18.

stichs.en: A song of ascents.
LORD, remember for David all his affliction,

verses.summary: The psalm opens by asking God to remember, and what is to be remembered is not David's merit but his hardship. The request is filed before any argument for it is made.

stichs.en: how he swore to the LORD, vowed
to the Mighty One of Jacob:

verses.summary: The content of the memory is an oath. This verb returns in verse 11 with the parties reversed, and that reversal is what joins the two halves of the psalm.

stichs.en: I will not come into the tent of my house,
I will not go up onto the couch of my bed,

verses.summary: Hebrew oaths are stated as half a sentence. The word opening each line means if, and the curse that would complete it is left unsaid, so the effect in English is a flat refusal.

stichs.en: I will not give sleep to my eyes,
slumber to my eyelids,

verses.summary: Sleep and slumber, eyes and eyelids: the second line narrows the first. The self denial is total but domestic, a man refusing his own bed rather than performing a feat.

stichs.en: until I find a place for the LORD,
dwellings for the Mighty One of Jacob.

verses.summary: The point of the sleeplessness. A place for God is the object of the whole vow, and the wording keeps both the ark and the city unnamed.

stichs.en: Look, we heard of it in Ephrathah;
we found it in the fields of the forest.

verses.summary: The voice turns plural and becomes a search party. Two place names, both of them contested, mark where the thing was heard of and where it was found.

stichs.en: Let us come to His dwellings,
let us bow down at the footstool of His feet.

verses.summary: The procession starts moving. Two cohortative verbs, let us come and let us bow, put the singer inside the crowd rather than in front of it.

stichs.en: Arise, LORD, to Your resting place,
You and the ark of Your strength.

verses.summary: The line borrows the formula spoken whenever the ark set out in the wilderness, with rest put where travel used to be. The journey is being declared over.

stichs.en: Let Your priests be clothed in righteousness,
and let Your faithful ones sing out.

verses.summary: The first of the two requests that get answered later. Note exactly what is asked for here, righteousness, and hold it against what arrives in verse 16.

stichs.en: For the sake of David Your servant,
do not turn away the face of Your anointed.

verses.summary: The plea rests entirely on someone else. David is long dead, and the whole argument is that a promise made to him is still owed to whoever sits in his place.

stichs.en: The LORD swore to David a truth
from which He will not turn back:
of the fruit of your body I will set on your throne.

verses.summary: The pivot of the psalm. The verb of verse 2 comes back with the parties exchanged: now God is the one swearing, and David is the one sworn to. Everything after this is answer, not request.

stichs.en: If your sons keep My covenant, and this testimony of Mine that I teach them,
their sons too, for ever, shall sit on your throne.

verses.summary: A condition attached to an oath that the previous verse called unturnable. Whether the grant is absolute or conditional is read both ways, and the psalm itself does not settle it.

stichs.en: For the LORD has chosen Zion;
He desired it for His seat.

verses.summary: The reason underneath both oaths. Not that David found a place, but that God chose one, and the choosing is stated in the vocabulary of wanting.

stichs.en: This is My resting place for ever;
here I will dwell, for I have desired it.

verses.summary: God speaks in the first person for the first time. The resting place David went out looking for in verse 5 is claimed here, using the same word he used.

stichs.en: I will greatly bless her provision;
I will satisfy her needy with bread.

verses.summary: The blessing begins with food, and with the poor. Before priests, kings or crowns, the city gets provisions and its needy get fed.

stichs.en: Her priests I will clothe in salvation,
and her faithful ones will shout aloud for joy.

verses.summary: The answer to verse 9, and it does not match the request. Righteousness was asked for and salvation is given, and the shout is doubled by an emphatic verb form.

stichs.en: There I will make a horn sprout for David;
I have set out a lamp for My anointed.

verses.summary: Two royal images, a horn that sprouts and a lamp kept ready. Both are living things: the dynasty is described as a plant and a flame, never as a building.

stichs.en: His enemies I will clothe in shame,
but on him his crown will gleam.

verses.summary: The clothing verb runs a third time, and this time it dresses the opposition. The psalm ends on a contrast rather than on a request.

pardes.body: Two halves, hinged on one verb. Verses 1 to 10 are the human side: a vow not to rest until God has a place, a search at {{6.2}} and {{6.5}}, a procession, and a plea that leans on a dead king's name. Verses 11 to 18 are the reply, spoken by God, and each request of the first half comes back altered. The prayer at {{8.0}} takes the words said whenever the ark set out in the wilderness and swaps the destination from marching to rest. Verses 8 to 10 appear again at the close of Solomon's dedication prayer in 2 Chronicles 6, which places this psalm in the world of the Temple rather than the road.

Three grammatical details carry the argument. First, the oaths at {{3.0}} and {{12.0}} open with the word if and never finish the sentence: a biblical oath cuts itself off before the self curse, so if I enter my house means I certainly will not. Second, the verb for clothing runs at {{9.1}}, {{16.1}} and {{18.1}}, and the garment differs each time, so the request is granted, upgraded, then turned on the enemies. Third, {{15.1}} sets an infinitive beside its own finite verb, the ordinary Hebrew way of saying that the thing will happen and there is no arguing about it. The two place names of verse 6 are disputed: Ephrathah is usually read as the region of Bethlehem and the fields of {{6.5}} as Kiriath-Jearim, where the ark stood before David moved it, but that identification is an inference from the names and is not stated in the psalm.

The tension readers keep returning to is between {{11.0}}, an oath God says He will not turn back from, and the condition in verse 12 that hangs the throne on whether David's sons keep the covenant. One line of reading takes the promise as unconditional and the condition as governing only unbroken rule; another takes the whole grant as conditional and the exile as its proof. Both readings are old, and this psalm does not decide between them. Verse 10 is the classic text for arguing from the merit of someone already dead: the petitioner offers nothing of his own and asks only that an old commitment be honoured. Chronicles puts that same sentence in Solomon's mouth at the moment the Temple is dedicated, which is a use of the psalm rather than a comment on it.

The controlling word is rest. It is the destination in {{8.0}} and God's own claim in verse 14, and in the mystical reading rest is not the absence of work but the state in which presence settles into a place and stops moving, which is why the same root names what the Sabbath is for. Zion is chosen by desire at {{13.4}} and desired again at {{14.7}}, so the longing runs in both directions and the dwelling is something wanted before it is something built. The crown of the last verse blossoms rather than shines, which keeps the king inside the same vocabulary of growth already used for the horn and the lamp.
